entities.name: Community
entities.tagline: Work done in public — a talk, a seat, a working group, a published case.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period whose output is addressed to people outside the organization paying for it: a
conference talk, a board or committee seat, a standards or user group, a case study published
under someone else's name. `organization` names the host — the conference, the group, the
publisher — not an employer.

A one-off writes `end` equal to `start`; a seat held over years does not. Both are this kind:
what makes it community work is the audience, not the duration.

entities.name: Education
entities.tagline: A degree, a certification, a course.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period whose output is a qualification rather than a delivery. `organization` names the
awarding body — the school, the certifying institute — which is the one case where the field
does not name somewhere work was done.

Learning that happened during a role is not this kind. Every role teaches something; what makes
a period education is that the qualification is the point of it.

entities.name: Project
entities.tagline: A delivery worth naming on its own, inside a role or beside one.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period defined by what it produced rather than by who it was spent with: a system, a
migration, a launch. Client work and internal work alike. `organization` names the client, or
the organization the work was done for when that differs from the employer.

It ends when the delivery does. A project that has no end and no deliverable is a role
described by its current work.

entities.name: Role
entities.tagline: A position held in an organization — the employment history.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
A period spent working for an organization under an arrangement that outlasts any one piece of
work: employment, a long-running contract, a partnership. `organization` names the employer.

It is not a delivery. What was built during a role belongs to a project, and a role that lists
one delivery in its achievements is usually two periods written as one. The test is whether the
period would have continued had the work changed: if it would, it is a role.

entities.name: Beacon Systems
entities.tagline: Billing software for companies whose pricing outgrew their spreadsheets.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
We build and run the billing platform our customers invoice their own customers through. Two
teams, one product, and a domain we are still splitting into the shapes it wants to be in.

We sell to companies at the point where pricing has become a system rather than a page —
usage, tiers, credits, corrections — and where getting an invoice wrong costs more than the
invoice.

entities.name: Competent
entities.tagline: Reliable alone. Unsupervised work with a predictable result.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Someone at this level works with it unsupervised and the result is predictable. They recognize
the common failure modes, having run into them.

entities.name: Expert
entities.tagline: Knows the limits. Has worked below the surface, shaped it, or taught it.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Someone at this level knows where it breaks down and where it is simply wrong. They have worked
below its surface, shaped it, or taught it.

entities.name: Familiar
entities.tagline: Needs support. Real use, with guidance or frequent reference.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Someone at this level has used it on real work, with guidance or frequent reference. They can
follow a conversation about it and make sense of other people's work in it.

entities.name: Proficient
entities.tagline: Exercises judgment. Chooses between alternatives and can say why.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Someone at this level makes judgment calls in it and can explain why the alternatives are
worse. Other people bring them their questions.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text:
Eight years across two companies, both of them small enough that the boundary between
building a thing and running it never really existed.

entities.name: Rebuilding the order pipeline
entities.tagline: Four years replacing a nightly batch with something that ran when the order did.

sections.heading: Achievements
sections.text:
- Replaced a nightly batch with a pipeline that ran when the order did, taking visibility from
  the next morning to seconds.
- Established that the speed-up mattered less than anyone expected, and why — which set the
  direction for the work that followed.

sections.heading: Ending
sections.text:
Left in January 2022 when the pipeline work was done and the next problem worth four years was
somewhere else.

entities.name: Splitting the billing domain
entities.tagline: Ongoing. Taking one service that three teams edited and making it two, each owned by one team.

sections.heading: Achievements
sections.text:
- Split one service that three teams edited into two that one team each owns, so the second
  team stopped waiting on the first to merge.
- Not finished: the third team is still waiting.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text:
Six years across the same two companies as the engineers he works with, on the other side of
the table: deciding what gets built rather than building it.

entities.name: Finding out what the order pipeline was for
entities.tagline: Three years learning that the speed-up nobody had asked for was still the right thing to build.

sections.heading: Achievements
sections.text:
- Ran the conversations that showed visibility, not speed, was what the pipeline rebuild
  bought — and rewrote the roadmap around it.
- Retired a reporting feature with no users, which was harder than shipping one.

entities.name: Conference talk — the speed-up nobody asked for
entities.tagline: A talk about a rebuild whose measured win was not the one it had been funded for.

sections.heading: Achievements
sections.text:
- Told a room that had funded the same kind of rebuild what the Northwind conversations
  found: that visibility, not speed, was what the pipeline bought.

entities.name: Deciding which billing goes first
entities.tagline: Ongoing. Choosing which of the two billing contexts serves customers first, and saying why.

sections.heading: Achievements
sections.text:
- Ranked the two contexts by what customers asked about in support, not by what was easier to
  split, and got the order accepted.
- Not finished: the third team's context has no customer voice yet, and no ranking.

entities.name: Domain-Driven Design
entities.tagline: Modeling software around the language the business already speaks.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
Name things as the business names them, and refuse a name that only makes sense inside the
codebase. Draw the boundary between one model and the next, and hold it when a second team
wants to reach across it. Rework the model when the language changes, rather than mapping
around it and keeping both.

entities.name: Java Programming
entities.tagline: Building and maintaining server-side systems on the JVM.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
Write services other teams depend on, and keep them running once they do. Read the stack trace
when one stops. Know the runtime well enough to tell a slow query from a slow collector, and to
say which of the two a graph is showing. Typical tools: the JDK, a build tool, a profiler.

entities.name: Product Discovery
entities.tagline: Finding out what is worth building before building it.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
Talk to the people who would use a thing before the first line of it is written. Frame the
question so that the answer can be no, and hear it when it is. Test the cheapest version of an
idea that could still turn out wrong, and stop when it does.

entities.name: Google Workspace
entities.tagline: The company's directory and documents; people and groups are synced from here. A `source-id` is the directory's user id.

entities.name: Local
entities.tagline: Written and kept in this repository; nothing syncs it.

entities.name: Partner directory
entities.tagline: The listing a buyer reaches from the directory's search, maintained by hand because the

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.text:
- **Company name and one-line description** — the identity's H1 and its tagline, unchanged.
- **The long description** — the identity's `## What it is`, cut to the directory's limit.
- **Capabilities** — the skills held at Proficient or Expert, under their own names.
- **Contact** — the identity's `email` and `url`.

sections.heading: Projection rules
sections.text:
- The long description is the identity's `## What it is` up to the limit below, cut at a
  paragraph and never mid-sentence. Nothing is written for the directory that is not in the
  model first.
- Capabilities carry no proficiency level. The directory shows a flat list and a level beside
  a name it does not explain reads as a grade, so the level decides which skills appear rather
  than appearing itself.
- Skills held at Familiar or Competent are left out. The listing is what the company sells, and
  a capability still being learned is not.
- No profile is named. The directory lists companies, and a person named here would be a fact
  about the company that the company's own identity does not carry.

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.text:
- The long description is at most 600 characters, the directory's limit, read from its editor
  on 2026-01-05.
- Every capability named is a skill in the model, spelled as that skill's H1.
- The contact address resolves to the company and not to a person.

entities.name: Craftsmanship
entities.tagline: We would rather ship one thing that holds up than three that need watching.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
We refuse a deadline that can only be met by leaving something half-built, and we say so early
enough that the date can still move.

We never ship on time while knowing privately which part will be rewritten within the quarter.

entities.name: Say The Hard Thing
entities.tagline: Disagreement that arrives after the decision is not disagreement, it is commentary.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.text:
We name the objection in the room where the choice is being made, once and plainly, and then
commit to whatever is decided.

We never agree in the meeting and reopen the question in a side channel afterwards.

entities.name: Billing nobody has to explain
entities.tagline: A customer reading one of our invoices can tell how the number was reached, without calling us and without a spreadsheet beside it.

sections.heading: What it means
sections.text:
Every charge traces to something the customer did, in language they used when they agreed to
it. When an invoice is disputed the answer is in the invoice, and support confirms it rather
than reconstructing it. We would know this holds when disputes are resolved by reading rather
than by investigation.

It says nothing about what we charge or whom we sell to. Pricing models and market are
decisions we expect to change several times; this is what we want to be true of the bill
whatever they turn out to be.
